content: All HIV-infected infants and children under 60 months of age should begin antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of their clinical or immunological status. If viral testing is unavailable, infants under 18 months with a presumptive severe HIV diagnosis should start ART, with confirmation of HIV infection obtained as soon as possible. For children aged 60 months or older, ART should be initiated if their CD4 count is below 500 cells/mm³, with priority given to those with a CD4 count ≤ 350 cells/mm³. The decision to start ART should also consider the child’s social environment, including the presence of a caregiver who understands the prognosis of HIV and the requirements of ART. In some cases, ART initiation may be delayed until the child is stabilized from acute infections. For children with confirmed or presumptive tuberculosis (TB), TB treatment should be prioritized, and ART should be started within the first eight weeks of TB therapy, as soon as it is tolerated. For children on TB treatment, those older than three years and weighing at least 10 kg should preferably receive a regimen containing efavirenz (EFV). For children under three years on a lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) regimen, consider adding ritonavir (RTV) in a 1:1 ratio with LPV to achieve a full therapeutic dose. Alternatively, a triple NNRTI-containing regimen may be used. The response to ART and potential side effects should be regularly monitored in all children receiving treatment. This includes reassessment of clinical status, laboratory parameters, and symptoms of drug toxicity. Common side effects of antiretroviral drugs include headache, abdominal pain, anemia, hypersensitivity reactions, and liver toxicity, among others. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), a condition associated with immune recovery after ART initiation, may occur, particularly in children with low CD4 levels. IRIS often resolves spontaneously or with anti-inflammatory drugs, but severe cases may require corticosteroids or temporary discontinuation of ART. Children on ART should be monitored for adherence to therapy and the need for additional support. Clinical follow-ups should occur at least every three months, with more frequent visits for clinically unstable children. Long-term follow-up should include regular assessments of growth, neurological development, and infection frequency. ART regimens may need to be adjusted in cases of treatment failure, which can be identified through clinical, immunological, or virological criteria. If treatment failure is confirmed, switching to a second-line regimen with at least three new drugs, including one from a new class, is necessary. HIV-exposed infants and children should receive all vaccines in the national immunization schedule, including Haemophilus influenzae type B and pneumococcal vaccines. However, the BCG vaccine should not be given to children known to be HIV-infected due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be provided to all HIV-exposed infants starting at 4–6 weeks of age and continued until HIV infection is excluded. In HIV-infected children, co-trimoxazole should be continued until they are five years old and on ART with sustained CD4 levels > 25%. Nutritional support is critical for HIV-infected children. Mothers are encouraged to exclusively breastfeed for six months and continue breastfeeding up to one year while on ART. Older children should consume energy-rich, varied diets to meet their nutritional needs. Children with severe acute malnutrition should be managed according to standard guidelines and provided with additional energy-rich foods. Management of HIV-related conditions, such as tuberculosis, pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), and fungal infections, should follow specific protocols. For example, HIV-infected children with active TB should begin TB treatment immediately, and those with PCP should receive high-dose co-trimoxazole promptly. Oral and esophageal candidiasis should be treated with antifungal agents like nystatin or fluconazole. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV is essential. HIV-infected pregnant women should receive lifelong ART to benefit their health and prevent transmission to their infants during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding while on ART significantly reduces the risk of HIV transmission. Mothers should be supported in making informed feeding decisions, balancing the prevention of HIV transmission with the nutritional needs of their infants. HIV-infected children may require referral for further investigations, second-line treatment, or counseling if necessary facilities are unavailable locally.
